query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Minor boron doping during processing induces beneficial segregation at the lamellar colony interfaces, which in turn both strengthens the interface and delays microcrack initiation, thereby improving both the yield strength and room-temperature tensile ductility of the eutectic high‐entropy alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that, under conventional processing, exhibit internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation under room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a low level (e.g., 0.1–0.5 atomic percent) of boron during alloy processing so that boron segregates to the colony interfaces.
generation.conditions: The alloy must be processed under identical conditions aside from the boron addition to preserve the eutectic lamellar structure; doping levels should be low enough to avoid forming brittle boride phases.
generation.structural_mediator: Boron atoms segregated at the internal (interlamellar) boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Boron segregates to the colony interfaces during processing, enhancing interface cohesion and reducing local stress concentration. This mechanism decreases the propensity for microcrack nucleation while simultaneously providing an interface-strengthening effect—thus countering the conventional trade-off between strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the undoped baseline, the boron-doped alloy should exhibit increased yield strength and enhanced tensile ductility at room temperature, as evidenced by a lower density of microcracks initiating at the interfaces.
generation.baseline: Performance of conventionally processed eutectic high-entropy alloys, which typically show high strength at the expense of ductility due to early microcrack formation along their internal lamellar boundaries.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only within a narrow dopant window; excessive boron content could induce the formation of brittle boride phases that may compromise ductility, while too little may not achieve effective segregation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise degree of improvement in strength and ductility, and the optimal boron concentration, remain to be quantified; the segregation kinetics under standard processing conditions also warrant further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples with identical processing parameters aside from boron content: one set with 0.1–0.5 at.% boron and one undoped. Characterize the microstructure using TEM and EDS mapping to verify boron segregation, and perform standardized room-temperature tensile tests to compare yield strength, tensile ductility, and crack initiation behavior between the two sets.
measurements: Tensile ductility (fracture strain from tensile tests)
Microcrack initiation density (observed via high-resolution microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in both yield strength and tensile ductility compared to the undoped baseline, or if boron does not preferentially segregate to the colony interfaces, then the hypothesis is falsified.
